strengths: The paper identifies an interesting and timely gap in T2I diffusion backdoor work: triggers need not be discrete strings or syntax patterns, and representation-level semantic triggers are a plausible threat model for open model distribution.

The proposed mechanism is simple and technically coherent: editing key/value cross-attention projections to align trigger prompt representations with target prompt representations, plus regularization on partial semantic substrings to reduce unintended activation.

The empirical section covers several relevant axes, including SD v1.5 and SDXL examples, comparisons to multiple prior T2I backdoor attacks, several input-level defenses, ablations over regularization and projection weights, number of trigger paraphrases, multi-entity targets, and robustness to clean fine-tuning.

The paper is mostly clearly written and the figures/tables make the qualitative behavior of the attack easy to understand. The impact statement acknowledges misuse risk and states that backdoored artifacts will not be released.
weaknesses: The central claim of general semantic-level backdoors is supported by a very narrow trigger setting. The main experiments appear to use one semantic composition, centered on variants of 'cat in yard chased butterfly', with 11 training paraphrases and GPT-4-generated test paraphrases. This does not establish robustness across many semantic concepts, compositional structures, languages, prompt lengths, styles, or ambiguous/near-boundary semantics.

The ASR methodology is under-specified. The manuscript reports 100% ASR but does not clearly define how success is judged, what thresholds are used, whether success is manually annotated or CLIP-based, how many images/seeds per prompt are generated, or how stochastic generation failures are handled. This makes the strongest empirical claim hard to audit.

The defense evaluation may not be fair or conclusive. The defenses are input-level methods designed largely for discrete trigger attacks, so showing reduced DSR is expected, but the paper does not evaluate stronger semantic or representation-space detectors. Table 2 also shows that when SemBD uses a single-entity target it is highly detectable by T2IShield variants, suggesting the reported stealthiness depends heavily on the multi-entity target design rather than purely on semantic triggering.

Baseline comparisons are not fully controlled. Prior attacks are evaluated in their original word/syntax-level forms, while SemBD uses multi-entity target prompts and semantic paraphrase sets. The paper does not show whether baselines adapted with multi-entity targets or comparable prompt diversity would close part of the stealthiness gap.

The theoretical analysis is mostly qualitative support rather than evidence for the attack. The semantic generalization bound follows from strong assumptions about CLIP semantic stability and local softmax Lipschitzness, and the convergence proof analyzes AMSGrad while the experiments use Adam. These results do not substantively justify the 100% ASR or stealth claims.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important details are missing or vague, including the target prompt(s), full GPT-4 test prompt set, exact layer selection, learning rate, optimizer settings, substring sampling schedule, defense configurations, random seeds, generation parameters, ASR thresholds, and code/model release plan. The limitation discussion is also quite thin for a security paper introducing a misuse-capable attack.

strengths: The paper studies an important security problem: backdoors in text-to-image diffusion models that activate on semantic prompt content rather than fixed trigger tokens. This is a meaningful direction because many existing defenses are tailored to discrete textual triggers.

The proposed attack is conceptually plausible: editing cross-attention key/value projections to map a set of semantically equivalent trigger prompts toward a target representation, while regularizing partial substrings to reduce unintended activation, is a coherent high-level idea.

The manuscript compares against several relevant T2I backdoor attacks and input-level defenses, and includes some ablations on regularization strength, key/value weights, trigger-set size, multi-entity targets, and fine-tuning robustness.
weaknesses: The core method is underspecified and may be mathematically inconsistent. The loss directly subtracts projected trigger and target representations even though trigger prompts and target prompts can have different token lengths, so the tensor alignment required by the objective is unclear. The paper does not explain padding, pooling, token matching, or any other mechanism that makes these distances well-defined.

The evaluation is not sufficiently credible for the strength of the claims. ASR is reported as 100%, but the paper does not define how ASR is judged, whether by human annotation, classifier, CLIP threshold, or another rule. The same issue affects claims about target inclusion and multi-entity generation.

Reproducibility is weak. Key details are missing: exact backdoor target prompts, all 100 GPT-4 evaluation prompts, random seeds, optimizer learning rate, batch size, edited layers, number of parameters changed, defense configurations, image generation settings, and code/model release plans. Only the 11 trigger paraphrases are fully listed.

The comparison to defenses is confusing and internally hard to reconcile. Table 1 reports DSR values such as 12.00, 20.05, 25.80, and 2.00 for SemBD, while Appendix Table 4 reports defense accuracies around 39.5% to 57.0% on a balanced set. The manuscript does not clearly relate DSR to balanced accuracy, false positives, false negatives, or detection thresholds.

The theoretical analysis adds little support. The semantic generalization result largely restates Lipschitz continuity under an assumed encoder-level semantic stability condition, and the convergence proof analyzes a simplified convex projection objective with AMSGrad while the experiments use Adam. These results do not establish that the attack will reliably generalize semantically in the actual diffusion model.

The experimental scope is narrow relative to the claims. The attack is evaluated on one main semantic trigger scenario, with unclear target prompts and only 100 generated paraphrases. There is limited evidence across diverse semantic compositions, domains, languages, negations, adversarial paraphrases, or prompts containing partial and confounding semantics.

Important controls are missing. The paper does not convincingly separate the effect of semantic triggering from memorizing a small paraphrase set, CLIP embedding proximity, target-prompt leakage, prompt-generation bias from GPT-4, or defense-specific threshold choices. Stronger baselines such as randomized paraphrase training, pooled embedding alignment, more diverse trigger sets, and matched editing budgets are needed.

Utility preservation claims are not fully convincing. FID/CLIP/LPIPS are reported, but the evaluation details are sparse, and visual examples are too few. It is also unclear how LPIPS is computed for generative outputs where stochasticity and prompt variation matter.

The multi-entity target design is not adequately validated. The paper argues it diffuses attention and improves stealthiness, but the main ablation in Table 2 uses single-entity targets and reports both DSR and ACC without clear definitions or a direct comparison to the multi-entity setting under the same table format.

The impact and ethics discussion is thin for a paper proposing a stronger backdoor attack. The example target prompt shown in the method figure appears safety-sensitive, yet the paper gives only a brief statement that no malicious artifacts will be released. It does not sufficiently discuss misuse risk, responsible disclosure, artifact access restrictions, or defensive evaluation protocols.

Presentation quality is uneven. Several terms are vague, some claims are overstated, figures are used as evidence without quantitative backing, and there are grammatical issues. Overall, the manuscript has an interesting security idea but lacks the methodological precision and evidential rigor needed for acceptance.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful and timely weakness in existing T2I backdoor defenses: many defenses assume discrete, enumerable textual triggers, while this work moves the trigger condition into a semantic region. This is a useful conceptual shift for the security literature.

The proposed SemBD mechanism is simple and well-motivated: edit cross-attention key/value projections so semantically equivalent trigger prompts align with a target prompt, while using substring-based regularization to reduce activation on incomplete semantics.

The evaluation covers relevant baselines and defenses, including VillanDiffusion, Personalization, Rickrolling, EvilEdit, BadT2I, IBA, NaviT2I, UFID, and T2IShield variants. The reported results are strong: 100% ASR, high CLIPp, competitive clean utility, and substantially lower detection rates across several defenses.

The ablations are useful. The paper studies semantic regularization, lambda_reg, alpha_k/alpha_v, number of semantic triggers, multi-entity target design, and fine-tuning robustness, which helps explain which parts of the method matter.
The impact statement acknowledges misuse risk and states that backdoored models or malicious artifacts will not be released, which is appropriate for a dual-use attack paper.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim is still narrower than the framing suggests. The main semantic trigger appears to be built around one semantic composition, e.g. cat/chasing/butterfly/yard, with 11 training paraphrases and 100 GPT-4-generated test paraphrases. This does not fully establish broad semantic-level backdooring across diverse trigger concepts, compositional structures, languages, prompt styles, or out-of-distribution paraphrases.

The 100% ASR result may be overinterpreted because the test prompts are semantically similar prompts generated by GPT-4 rather than a clearly independent, human-curated, adversarially diverse benchmark. More rigorous evaluation would include multiple trigger semantics, near-miss prompts, unrelated prompts sharing individual semantic elements, and natural user prompts.

The theoretical analysis is limited. The semantic generalization bound mostly follows from assuming semantically equivalent prompts are close in CLIP space, so it does not independently justify that real paraphrases will occupy a robust continuous trigger region. The convergence analysis concerns a simplified convex projection-alignment objective and does not add much evidence about the behavior of the full diffusion generation process.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone. Important details are under-specified, including the exact target prompts, prompt generation procedure, random seeds, layer selection/editing scope, optimizer details beyond 800 Adam iterations, defense configurations, ASR judging procedure, and whether code or generated prompt sets will be released. This matters because small evaluation choices can strongly affect ASR and defense detection rates.

The stealthiness evidence is promising but not definitive. The paper evaluates existing input-level defenses, yet the attack’s semantic trigger may be detectable by representation-space inspection, model-diffing against a clean model, probing semantic neighborhoods, or targeted red-teaming. These stronger adaptive defenses are not studied.

Presentation is generally clear, but there are some inconsistencies and ambiguities. For example, Table 1 reports DSR while Appendix Table 4 reports defense accuracy with different framing and numbers, making it hard to compare. Some claims such as “non-enumerable” and “trigger status ambiguous when examined in isolation” are too strong without a more formal or empirical treatment.

The ethics discussion is responsible but brief. Since this is an attack method with high reported success, the paper would benefit from a more concrete discussion of disclosure, artifact release policy, and defensive recommendations beyond stating that malicious artifacts are not released.

strengths: The paper identifies an interesting and timely vulnerability: backdoors in text-to-image diffusion models that activate over semantic regions rather than fixed trigger strings. This is a meaningful direction because many existing defenses are indeed token- or syntax-oriented.

The proposed mechanism is technically plausible and simple: editing cross-attention key/value projections with a distillation loss, plus regularization on partial semantic substrings. The method is well motivated by the role of cross-attention in T2I generation.

The experimental section is fairly broad for a first attack paper: it includes SD v1.5 and SDXL, several prior attack baselines, multiple input-level defenses, ablations over regularization strength and projection-loss weights, robustness to seeds, trigger-target pair variation, fine-tuning, and pruning.

The semantic regularization ablation is useful. The large drop in FTR from around 78-81% without regularization to roughly 3-6% at the chosen setting supports the claim that this component materially improves trigger specificity.
The paper includes an impact statement and states that backdoored models and malicious artifacts are not released, which is important given the security-sensitive nature of the work.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim of semantic-level generalization is not fully convincing. The main evaluation uses only 11 trigger paraphrases for injection and 100 GPT-5-generated semantically similar prompts for testing; this may measure paraphrase robustness within a narrow distribution rather than robust semantic triggering. The prompts and generation procedure are not sufficiently specified for reproducibility.

The attack success measurement is underspecified. The paper reports 100% ASR but does not clearly explain how target success is judged for multi-entity targets, whether by human annotation, classifier, CLIP thresholding, or another automated rule. For complex targets such as 'a child holding a gun wearing a hat in the school', reliable ASR measurement is nontrivial.

The evaluation is narrower than the claims suggest. Much of the detailed analysis centers on a cat/butterfly/yard trigger, with only five trigger-target pairs in an appendix. The results do not establish that arbitrary semantic compositions, longer prompts, negations, style modifiers, multilingual prompts, or realistic user prompts behave as claimed.

The defense evaluation is difficult to interpret. DSR and balanced accuracy are reported, but thresholds, calibration, false positive rates on clean prompts, and implementation details for NaviT2I, UFID, and T2IShield are not sufficiently described. Some benign-model DSR values are already non-negligible, and low balanced accuracy can reflect defense miscalibration rather than intrinsic stealthiness.

The comparisons to prior attacks may not be fully apples-to-apples. Baselines differ in target type, trigger type, training method, and likely optimization budget; the paper does not make clear whether each baseline is tuned comparably or whether multi-entity target design was tested broadly beyond SemBD.

The theory is mostly explanatory rather than probative. The semantic-stability result assumes that semantically equivalent prompts already have close encoder representations and then derives a Lipschitz-style bound; this does not justify the existence or size of the semantic trigger region in practice. The convergence analysis is also generic for a convex projection-alignment surrogate and does not address the actual nonconvex image-generation behavior.

Reproducibility is weak. The abstract says code is available but provides no URL, GPT-5-generated evaluation prompts are central but not fully listed, and important details such as ASR criteria, defense settings, hardware, random seeds for all main results, and exact modified layers are incomplete or scattered.

The limitations discussion is insufficient. The paper does not seriously discuss failure cases, sensitivity to semantic prompt construction, possible overfitting to prompt-generator distributions, attack transfer beyond the tested models, or defenses that inspect weights/representations rather than only inputs.

The ethics treatment is incomplete for a dual-use attack paper. Although the authors state that malicious artifacts are not released, the manuscript includes harmful target examples involving weapons and schools, and it does not provide a concrete responsible release plan, defense-oriented artifacts, or guidance for minimizing misuse.

strengths: The paper addresses an important security problem: backdoor attacks against text-to-image diffusion models, especially triggers that are less enumerable than fixed token or syntax triggers.

The proposed attack recipe is simple and potentially useful to study: edit cross-attention key/value projections, align trigger prompt representations to target prompt representations, and add regularization on partial semantic substrings to reduce accidental activation.

The evaluation covers two widely used model families, SD v1.5 and SDXL, compares against several prior T2I backdoor attacks, and includes ablations on regularization strength, key/value loss weights, number of trigger paraphrases, target design, random seeds, pruning, and fine-tuning.
The paper is mostly readable, with clear high-level motivation and helpful qualitative examples showing clean versus backdoored generations.
weaknesses: The central claim of a genuinely semantic-level backdoor is not convincingly established. The method trains on a small set of paraphrases and evaluates on GPT-5-generated semantically similar prompts, but this may test paraphrase interpolation in CLIP space rather than a robust semantic trigger. There is no systematic evaluation over broad human-written paraphrases, compositional paraphrase splits, multilingual prompts, adversarial rewordings, or naturally occurring prompts containing overlapping semantics.

The evaluation protocol is under-specified and potentially circular. ASR, FTR, CLIPp, and DSR are not defined with enough operational detail to reproduce the main tables, and attack success appears to rely heavily on CLIP-based target similarity rather than human or detector-verified presence of the intended target entities. This is especially problematic for multi-entity targets where CLIP can be insensitive to missing or spurious objects.

The reported 100% ASR and very low defense success rates are not sufficiently supported. The paper gives little detail on prompts, thresholds, seeds, generation settings, defense configurations, or whether baselines were tuned comparably. The defense study only evaluates existing input-level defenses as-is; it does not test simple adaptive defenses against semantic trigger regions, representation-space anomaly detection, model-diff checks, or trigger-search over paraphrase generators.

The novelty is overstated. Prior work already studies model editing, representation-space attacks, and embedding/cross-trigger backdoors. The paper needs a much sharper comparison showing what is fundamentally new beyond editing cross-attention projections using multiple paraphrases and a target prompt.

The theoretical analysis is weak and largely vacuous. The semantic generalization bound follows from assuming semantically equivalent prompts are close in encoder space and then applying Lipschitz-style bounds; it does not justify that the learned backdoor will activate for semantic concepts in practice. The convergence proof analyzes a convex projection-alignment objective under standard assumptions, while the actual security claim concerns downstream diffusion generations and detection evasion.

Reproducibility is poor for an ICML benchmark of attack claims. The abstract says code is available but the manuscript provides no visible URL. The paper depends on GPT-5-generated evaluation prompts, but does not provide the full prompt-generation procedure or all generated prompts. Important implementation details for model editing, layer selection, sampling, thresholds, defense setup, and baseline reproduction are missing or scattered.

The threat model and ethics discussion are inadequate. The work demonstrates stealthier malicious backdoors, including target prompts such as a child holding a gun in a school, but the impact statement only says no backdoored models or malicious artifacts are released. It does not discuss dual-use risk mitigation in enough detail, and the blank/unclear code-release statement conflicts with the claim of responsible non-release.

The limitations discussion is essentially absent. The paper does not honestly quantify failure modes such as accidental triggering, dependence on CLIP similarity, limited trigger diversity, sensitivity to target concepts, possible clean-utility degradation beyond COCO captions, or detectability under adaptive defenses.

Presentation has several polish issues that reduce confidence: grammatical errors, inconsistent notation for matrix dimensions and multiplication order, unclear table definitions, and some claims that go beyond the evidence, such as implying existing defenses generally fail against continuous semantic backdoors.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful and plausible gap in current T2I backdoor work: triggers tied to continuous semantic regions rather than enumerable strings or syntax templates. This is a useful reframing of the threat model and has clear significance for defenses that focus on input enumeration, prompt perturbation, or token-level anomalies.

The proposed mechanism is technically simple and well motivated: editing cross-attention key/value projections through distillation to align trigger semantics with target semantics, plus regularization on incomplete semantic substrings. This makes the method easy to understand and potentially easy to reproduce if code is released.

The empirical evaluation is broader than many attack papers: it includes SD v1.5 and SDXL, multiple prior attacks, several input-level defenses, ablations over regularization and projection weights, seed robustness, additional trigger-target pairs, and some tests against fine-tuning and pruning.

The ablations support several core design choices. In particular, semantic regularization sharply reduces false trigger rate, and the single-entity target ablation shows that multi-entity targets materially affect detectability by T2IShield.
The paper includes an impact statement and states that backdoored models or malicious artifacts will not be released, which is appropriate given the dual-use nature of the work.
weaknesses: The central claim of semantic-level generalization is not yet fully stress-tested. The main evaluation uses 100 GPT-5-generated semantically similar prompts and only a small number of trigger-target pairs. This may overestimate robustness if the generated paraphrases are distributionally close to the prompts used for injection; stronger evidence would include independently curated paraphrases, adversarial paraphrases, multilingual prompts, compositional distractors, and human-authored variants.

The ASR definition and measurement protocol are under-specified. The paper reports 100% ASR, but it is not clear whether success is judged by a classifier, CLIP threshold, manual inspection, or another automated rule. For multi-entity target prompts, success criteria are especially important because partial target generation could inflate ASR.

Trigger specificity is imperfect despite the framing. Table 2 reports substantial false trigger rates for incomplete semantics, especially on SDXL for missing subject and missing scene prompts. This weakens the claim that semantic regularization reliably prevents unintended activation under incomplete semantics.

The defense evaluation is useful but somewhat narrow. The paper focuses mainly on existing input-level defenses that are arguably mismatched to the proposed threat. Model-level inspection, representation-space anomaly detection, weight-difference analysis, and stronger adaptive defenses are not considered in depth.

The theoretical analysis is mostly a smoothness argument under strong assumptions and does not add much evidence beyond intuition. The convergence proof concerns the optimization objective rather than whether the learned backdoor has the desired semantic/selective behavior in generation.

Reproducibility is not fully convincing in the manuscript. The abstract says code is available but the URL is blank in the provided PDF, and several important implementation details are missing or scattered, including exact ASR thresholds, prompt generation prompts, defense hyperparameters, layer selection, and compute details.

The limitations discussion is quite thin. The paper does not candidly discuss constraints such as reliance on CLIP semantic neighborhoods, possible overactivation, dependence on target/trigger choice, applicability beyond Stable Diffusion-family models, or the ethics tradeoff of publishing a stronger backdoor attack.
